summary: Describes scenarios where it is hard to work out which policy to apply to a host, which the document calls host identification. Collecting these scenarios helps find commonalities before solutions are designed.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of confusing situations where the network cannot tell which kid is which, so it cannot apply the right rules.

questions: how to identify hosts behind nat
subtitle: When networks can't tell which host is which behind a shared address

tldr.problem: As networks evolve, multiple scenarios appear where one public IP address represents many private hosts, making it impossible to identify individual hosts for applying policies or services.
tldr.mechanism: This document catalogs seven major deployment scenarios and variations where host identification breaks down, from carrier-grade NAT to mobile network convergence, analyzing their common root causes.
tldr.outcome: The collection of scenarios provides a foundation for designing solutions to identify individual hosts and apply per-host policies in these complex deployments.

today: RFC 7620 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It remains the reference for understanding host identification complications in modern network deployments.

sections.title: The Host Identification Problem
sections.content:
This document addresses a fundamental challenge in modern networks: uniquely identifying individual hosts when multiple devices share a single public IP address. This situation occurs in many real-world deployments, and causes practical problems for network operators who want to apply policies, enforce access controls, or provide specific services to individual users.

Three root causes produce these identification issues: address sharing (common in NAT deployments), the use of tunnels between administrative domains, or a combination of both. Understanding which deployments suffer from these problems is the first step toward designing solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks assign IP addresses to identify machines, but sometimes many machines share one address. The document describes when this happens and why it is a problem.

sections.title: Major Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) consolidates many customers' networks behind a single IP address visible to the Internet. Remote servers cannot distinguish between hosts sharing that address, breaking access control and abuse detection. Address plus Port (A+P) assigns each subscriber the same IPv4 address but with different port ranges, achieving address sharing without a NAT function at the provider edge, yet still preventing remote servers from identifying individual hosts.

Application proxies (on-premise or distributed) sit between clients and servers, forwarding traffic on behalf of multiple internal hosts. Servers see only the proxy's address. Overlay networks use similar NAT operations to intercept and optimize traffic, masking the true endpoints. Emergency services face a specific variant of this: when a caller behind a NAT or VPN makes an emergency call, the service provider cannot determine the caller's actual location from the source IP address alone.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists seven real situations where servers cannot tell which user is which, including shared home networks, mobile carriers routing traffic, business proxies, and systems that hide their users.

sections.title: Cellular and Enterprise Variants
sections.content:
Cellular networks allocate private IPv4 addresses to mobile devices and deploy NAT44 functions at the network boundary, facing the same identification challenges as CGN. Provider WLAN services present a variation: when visitors use an operator's public hotspot alongside a subscriber's home network, the operator cannot distinguish between the subscriber's traffic and the visitor's traffic if both are behind a shared NAT at the residential gateway.

Femtocell deployments, which graft home base stations into mobile networks, combine NAT, tunneling, and multiple administrative domains. Fixed and mobile network convergence scenarios require the fixed broadband network to retrieve policies from the mobile network for hosts that may share either IPv4 addresses (via NAPT) or IPv6 prefixes. These scenarios demonstrate that IPv6 deployment alone does not solve host identification when address sharing occurs within a single administrative domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile phones, home WiFi networks, and combinations of fixed and mobile networks all create situations where the network cannot see individual users.

sections.title: Root Causes and Synthesis
sections.content:
Analysis reveals that all scenarios stem from three root causes: address sharing, tunneling between domains, or both in combination. A synthesis table in the document maps each scenario against these root causes and notes whether it applies to IPv4, IPv6, or both. Some scenarios are confined to a single administrative domain (making host identification a local concern), while others span multiple domains (introducing privacy and interoperability risks).

Understanding which root cause applies to each scenario helps solution designers choose appropriate mechanisms. For instance, solutions relying on bits of the source IP address and port number may expose privacy information differently depending on whether address sharing is within one domain or across multiple domains, or whether tunneling is involved.
sections.plainLanguage: The document groups the scenarios by what causes them: sharing addresses, using tunnels, or both. This helps engineers design fixes that target the right problem.

sections.title: Privacy and Scope
sections.content:
The document emphasizes that host identification solutions should not reveal information beyond what the original packet would have already exposed. Operators may use bits of the source IP address or port number to restore host identity within their domain, but such mechanisms must not enable privacy circumvention—for instance, nullifying a subscriber's use of address sharing to anonymize their traffic.

The scope excludes purely proprietary headers and focuses exclusively on means to recover information conveyed in the original packet. This ensures that solutions remain compatible with the Internet's filtering and policy infrastructure while respecting users' privacy expectations where address sharing was chosen as a privacy tool.
sections.plainLanguage: When fixing the identification problem, solutions should not expose more than the original packet already revealed, and should not undo privacy protections that users chose.
